tagline: Up the west shore of what is left of Lake Lahontan.
intro: SR 445 comes north out of Sparks, narrows to two lanes and enters the Pyramid Lake Indian Reservation. There it swings northwest along the western shore of Pyramid Lake, through Sutcliffe to Warrior Point. The stretch inside the reservation is the byway, beside a desert lake that the Federal Highway Administration says turns from green to turquoise to deep blue.

The Truckee River feeds it, mostly with Lake Tahoe's outflow, and only evaporation and seepage take water away. It is the biggest remnant of ancient Lake Lahontan. John C. Frémont named it for a tufa rock shaped like a pyramid. The Paiute name it for the cui-ui, a fish that lives nowhere else.

moments.title: Sutcliffe
moments.text: The settlement on the byway, 282 people on the lake's western bank, a little under six miles across the water from the Pyramid.

moments.title: Anaho Island
moments.text: The lake's largest tufa formation, about a mile across, is a refuge for a colony of American white pelicans. No boat may come within 1,000 feet of its shore.

moments.title: The Pyramid
moments.text: The small tufa island that gave the lake its English name. A white band of calcium carbonate to its east marks where the water stood when the lake was near overflowing.

practical: A day-use permit is required for camping, swimming, fishing, hiking, picnicking or driving off-road, and the north and east sides of the lake have been closed to non-members since 2011.
